column28: •	Conservative forest extent: The mapped ~3.26 billion ha likely underestimates true forest area due to strict rules designed to avoid false positives, excluding many borderline or uncertain areas. •	Threshold-related exclusions: Combining a ≥5 m tree height threshold with tree cover masks removes substantial forest areas (e.g., regions with lower canopy cover), meaning some valid forests may be omitted. •	Exclusion of certain forest types: Planted forests are intentionally excluded, and young or regenerating forests (expected to meet forest criteria) are often missing due to lack of reliable data. •	Disturbance-related misclassification: Some naturally disturbed forests (e.g., from fire or wind) may be wrongly excluded because it is difficult to distinguish natural from human-driven disturbances using EO data. •	Inclusion errors remain possible: Some non-natural systems (e.g., agroforestry or planted trees not captured in plantation datasets) may still be incorrectly included. •	Uncertainty in forest classes: Old secondary forests are particularly uncertain, as they are largely defined by exclusion (i.e., not primary or young), making this class heterogeneous and less reliable. •	Dependence on input datasets: The classification fully relies on the quality and agreement of multiple underlying datasets, each with its own limitations and inconsistencies. •	Lack of validation data: There is no independent global reference dataset to rigorously validate the classification, limiting confidence in its accuracy. •	Conceptual ambiguity: Definitions of forest types (e.g., “primary forest”) vary in the literature, making it difficult to ensure that EO-based classifications truly reflect ecological reality.

column28: •	Classification boundary uncertainty: Forest type separation is inherently uncertain because classes (e.g., primary vs. naturally regenerating forest) are inferred from indirect satellite proxies, and mature secondary forests can look identical to primary forests. Planted forests and agroforestry systems are especially difficult, often overlapping spectrally with other forest types and leading to misclassification. •	Definition-related ambiguity: FAO-based definitions include management intent and temporary states (e.g., harvested but unstocked plantations), which cannot be directly observed in satellite data; as a result, some areas classified as “other land” may still meet forest definitions. •	Temporal limitations: The map represents conditions for 2020 using annual composites, so late-year changes and recent disturbances (e.g., fires, logging) may be missed or misclassified, particularly in post-fire recovery areas. •	Spatial resolution constraints: At 10 m resolution, mixed pixels and small-scale heterogeneity (e.g., smallholder landscapes or narrow forest patches) can lead to ambiguous or inconsistent classification near thresholds. •	Calibration limitations: Reported class probabilities are ensemble outputs without full post-hoc calibration, meaning they may not represent true probabilistic confidence and may require additional regional calibration for precise quantitative use.
